b:
I guess I didn't make myself clear.

As of now, I do believe that homosexuality is sinful according to divine laws. And I believe it is very important that followers of these laws obey them. However, it is not important that I go around telling the people around me how wrong they are. Unfortunately, many individuals have made it their business to tell LGBTQ+ people how wrong they are by saying very hateful things. That ignorant behavior has become so common that if I simply mention that I believe homosexuality is sinful, I may (almost always) get put in the same box with all those hateful people. In addition to that, my friend does not consider himself one of the faithful, so for me to tell him that he's not obeying divine laws would mean nothing to him except that he might think I'm looking down on him. So what I said was not merely an effort to avoid saying how I feel. I honestly said exactly what I think. There are lots of things that matter. My stance on this issue is one of those things that matters, but there are more important things to talk about.

I did not downplay it. Prior to this, I had spent about an hour consoling him about his dad (who had said some very hateful things about his sexuality) and ensuring him that I love him even if other people are hateful.

That's why they asked the question, and, as you said, after numerous attempts to avoid the question, you still avoided answering it honestly. Why would you continually make efforts to avoid that question? Are you that insecure about where you stand?

I did not make attempts to skirt the question. I made attempts to avoid the conversation (about whether or not homosexuality is sinful), because many already say far too much on the subject. But since he asked, I did answer honestly. I told him exactly what I think. And I am very secure about where I stand. I have approached the issue very torn and open-minded, and, after much deliberation and reflection, I conclusively gathered that homosexuality is sinful. But I also concluded that we (followers of these beliefs) should be focusing on all the positive effects of a relationship with the divine - not all the things that the people around us are doing wrong.

I try to focus on the positive things in life. And I believe that, by doing that, the negative will have no room to grow.

That is not asinine.

I was not dishonest. Everything I said is exactly what I think and how I feel. You should know that in response, he thanked me for my honesty and open-mindedness.

> So your stance is important, just not important enough to talk about when your friend asks?

Yes, exactly. My friend wanted to know if I was going to one day reveal that I had secretly hated him for being gay like his father did. I believe that having a relationship with a higher power and committing oneself to participate in the community of like-minded individuals are more important than whether one is gay or not. He asked how I feel. I told him how I feel. Nothing dishonest about that.

What about that biblical verse? I am a part of the Kingdom of God, but I'm in this world. So how can you say that the Kingdom of God is not of this world? The ancient theocracy pleased God at times. In fact, there were periods when they were quite successful in doing God's will.

When I read the Old Testament, the pattern that I notice is that when the leadership fails to uphold Godly values, the people stray from God's ways. But when the leaders are Godly, the people follow God's ways. I would say rules and governance have a major effect on people's hearts.

It's not idolatrous to have human leadership. A higher power appointed several leaders over a community. They were given the authority they needed to guide the people as well as the qualities (e.g. wisdom, kindness, patience) they needed to avoid misusing their authority.

I believe it's something like this:

**Person A:** Hey, are you on my side or their side?

**Person B:** I'm on the side of a higher power. And I'm the leader of everyone on that side.

**Person A:** Oh ok. Well I definitely want to be on that side. I'll do whatever you say.

I've heard lots of sermons where the main point is, "You should be asking the higher power what it wants you to do - not telling it what you want." They try to come up with so many examples and analogies. I always wonder why they don't just use this story. It's directly applicable to daily life.

There's a difference between living in the world and trying to create a worldly government of the organized religious community, with, presumably, the enforcement of religious laws and morals on all citizens, even non-adherents.

But the kingdom of the divine only enforced its values on the people of the faith, including non-natives who had joined the community. But everyone else was considered an outsider and treated as such. Godly practices were not expected of outsiders.

The theocratic system failed, time and again.

But every time the followers ran into trouble, it was because they had strayed from the system that was set up. The system worked as long as the people followed it. The theocracy was a major success as long as it was adhered to.

I think everyone could benefit from the model of a good community found in various faith traditions. Admittedly, there are many organizations that don't set a very good example. But I'm talking about the ones that do it right.

Growing up in a supportive community has been beneficial to me in countless ways, but one really big one has been realizing the power of a group in which people love and support one another despite their vastly different backgrounds, circumstances, and perspectives. It's incredible to see how a group of people, who would otherwise probably never be in the same room together, can be drawn together by their common understanding that happiness comes from serving others and their common goal of pursuing that which they believe to be good and pure. Moreover, this community is made up of a broad cross-section of society, so it contains all kinds of skills and disciplines. Because of this, the community is capable of achieving great things, even with few resources, and while maintaining a humble attitude.

Of course, all of that I've described is not unique to any one group. This is how many ancient communities were designed to function long before modern times. What many teachings brought was a reminder that this community was not meant to be exclusive. They taught that the community of people should have an open-door policy for anyone who wanted to be a part of it (by both contributing and benefiting). I think the only thing that could be better than such a unified community is allowing others to join it.

It makes me so sad that there are entire organizations that don't understand this; they're missing the point completely. Then outsiders wonder why anyone would want to be a part of that. I wish everyone could experience it the way I have.

No. It's not critical to understand everything about the nature of a higher power. For instance, we could debate for a very long time about the shape and color of this higher power. One could argue that those attributes are part of its nature and therefore we should know them and believe in them. But most people don't waste their time with such trivial topics, because in the end it makes no difference what color or shape this higher power is. So simply saying that something is part of its nature does not give it some inherent importance. Similarly, I'm asking what makes the Trinitarian understanding of this higher power important? What difference does it make?

Of course you have to know **something** about them. You have to know many things about them. But there are also many things that you don't need to know. There are lots of trivial attributes of my nature (like the way some of the freckles on my arm almost form a straight line) that my partner does not need to know in order for us to maintain a good relationship. So what makes the Trinitarian understanding of a higher power one of the important things and not one of the trivial things?
Which part of the gospel necessitates the belief that Jesus is divine?
"If only you would be altogether silent! For you, that would be wisdom." -a divine being to a faithful servant

God's people were well-acquainted with divine forgiveness long before the significant event of the crucifixion. And regardless of the nature of the central figure, he lived a perfect life and died a sinner's death, which is a sufficient sacrifice. So it seems like the message of hope is still good news even if the central figure wasn't divine.

You mentioned that the aspect of the gospel that necessitates the divinity of the figure is the concept of divine self-sacrifice. I was highlighting that the divine can be loving and forgiving even if that figure wasn't divine - even if the divine didn't make a sacrifice.
Those are marvelous things if they are true. But even if they aren't, isn't he incredible and caring?

If you read the post, you'll see that that is exactly the reason that climate change should be a priority. Wealthy individuals are least susceptible to the effects of climate change. But the poor and marginalized are the ones suffering from it (in large numbers). It would be hypocritical for those who profess to care for others by "spreading their beliefs and witnessing to others," while simultaneously harming the same people.

We know that natural disasters are caused (at least in part) by factors that are within our control. For example, a significant environmental crisis in the 1930s was a series of three "natural disasters" (drought and dust storms) that were caused by agricultural practices not suited for arid conditions. The solution was to educate farmers on the proper way to cultivate land in such regions, and we haven't experienced a similar crisis since. The current climate change issue is analogous but affects a larger geographic area and spans a longer time scale.
Yeah, but I couldn't come up with a wording that I liked. I figured people would understand what I meant.
I would love to know why. Which of the points do you disagree with?

They differ in that one is physical and the other is metaphysical. If you're willing to accept that difference and compare them accordingly, then I think it's fair to say that the two are similar. If you doubt the metaphysical altogether, then this conversation would have to be very long.

If humanity is causing the problem, then what makes you think it's too big for humanity to fix? As pointed out in the post, humanity was made the steward of the world and its inhabitants.

> Before the earth goes beyond the tipping point and life on earth is threatened

As mentioned in the post, many thousands have already died and are dying still.

> Instead of getting involved in the world

Of all the wisdom in various teachings, none advocates for complacency. We are obligated to help the less fortunate, even when we played no role in their affliction. How much more when we are the source of their suffering!

I see. To an extent, I agree with you. I was careful not to say that addressing climate change should be anyone's **highest** priority. For example, stopping violent crime is something that requires a direct as well as indirect approach, and the direct approach may not always be resource-efficient. Same with caring for those in desperate need.

However, as the post points out, almost all of the actions that we can take to help the planet don't require the expenditure of resources. In fact, most of them will actually reduce expenses, which will free up resources for helping people more directly.

I can't think of a situation in which an organization's efforts to help people would prevent it from also helping the planet.
That's kinda the point of the original post. It first lays out the evidence. Then it explains the conclusions that are drawn from the evidence.

That sounds like a lot of excuses to not try. I don't know the effects of everyone changing their habits for the better, though it's hard for me to imagine any realistic negative consequences. However, I have examined my own life and noted every possible way for me to reduce my own carbon footprint, and I have begun to do so. And I expect others to do the same.
What do you interpret that verse to mean and how is it applicable?
By what definition of religion? I do not worship it and it does not detract from my worship of a higher power. In fact, I care for the planet as an act of service to that higher power.
I hope that if/when we implement some semblance of a solution to climate change, we will return to solve the root problem, which is this kind of mindset.

I think a significant figure attempted to address this in the parable where a man leaves his servants in charge. He expects that when he returns he will find that his servants are working and have been working in his absence. The servants shouldn't just sit around waiting for the master.

This is a really good question and I'm disappointed that it took so long for someone to ask it. When any person suggests that others should change their actions, that person should be asked to give an account of their own actions. Fewer people would tell others what to do if they knew they would be held to the same standard.

My partner and I were typical suburban American consumers. I am proud to say that when we realized we were part of the problem, we radically redesigned our lifestyle and left consumerism behind. The only way I could share this post was knowing that I'm not asking anyone to do anything that I haven't done myself.

But I'm not aligned with the left. So are my concerns legitimate or do you think I also have an agenda?

What is the left's agenda? Getting all the scientists in the world to accept climate change and fabricate evidence to support it seems like a huge gamble and an ineffective way to push an agenda.

You're right that the problem requires cooperation, but the first step is making personal changes. This is true for anyone trying to get others to take some action. You must first be an example. Then people are more likely to cooperate.

My detailed assessment in the original post does not use any politically motivated sources. The information is peer-reviewed and factual - not opinions.

I have done my best to fairly examine both political perspectives and it seems that both sides potentially have something to gain. Yes, some individuals use this issue purely for political gain, just like some people abuse their positions in religious institutions for selfish gain. You must look past that and assess the truth of the matter despite the human selfishness surrounding it.

There are three reasons.

1. I don't think the civil rights leader was wicked or deceptive. At worst, he was undecided.

2. Of the reasons that a prominent religious figure gave to despair or be angry, hell wasn't one. He directed his followers' attention toward their neighbor's wellbeing in this life - not their own wellbeing in the afterlife.

3. If anyone is in hell, it's not because someone else caused them to go there. It's no one's fault but their own.

For the sake of promoting discussion:

1. Isn't that what community leaders are for? If not community leaders, then close friends?

2. You could say the same for performers, but places of worship often have plenty of them, or they go out of their way to find them. Obviously, some places of worship would have trouble implementing this immediately, but if the community promoted learning useful skills in the same way as music, then I don't see why they would have trouble finding skilled labor among the members.

3. It would probably help to have a coordinator. But if that coordinator delegates to responsible individuals, he/she shouldn't have to commit much time to managing them. Even if it did take a lot of time, it doesn't have to be the same person all the time does it?

4. Why?

5. Oftentimes the community/staff is honest with its funds and there's no reason to doubt them. However, part of being equally supportive and bearing one another's burdens means I pick up the slack when my neighbor falls short, even if it's my neighbor's fault. Even if it's the fault of the doubter, I'm suggesting that the community could help by using donations to feed and clothe those in desperate need rather than pocket some of it.

6. Are you suggesting that it would be a lower quality service if responsibilities were shared or if it required less time?

Thank you.

I understand that you're interpreting this verse to mean money instead of honor, but why do you think that? In a society that values honor and shame, it's reasonable to think that honor here actually means honor.
But isn't everyone in the community expected to contribute? Why not compensate everyone?
That's a good distinction to make, but in your analogy, the group is made up of individuals who are also expected to contribute, so shouldn't they all receive compensation?

I wasn't trying to generalize. I understood your explanation to be this:

*The leader works by serving the community, so he should be compensated.*

Did I misunderstand?

I'm wondering why that can't apply to everyone who serves? Or, why can't his responsibilities be shared so that anyone could take them on in their spare time, thus freeing up resources to assist those in more urgent need?
At my current place of worship, a higher power does (not being facetious) and it seems to work pretty well.

It seems that you have missed the point of the post. I know that some individuals have chosen to serve their religious community instead of pursuing secular employment, and they expect to be compensated. What I'm saying is that this draws a lot of unnecessary negative attention, and it seems like we could avoid that if we would just divide the workload of service so **everyone** in the community (including leaders) is free to earn their own income instead of relying on donations.

What is the benefit? In what case would it be preferable to have one individual do the work of the entire community (and compensate them) instead of having the whole community engage in the work (and use the resources to assist those in need)?

Yes, but that salary is usually funded by the donations of the religious organization as I mentioned.

As I stated in the original post, couldn't the workload be divided so that you don't need a full-time leader?

I understand that in some parts of the world, most people lack the education or time to sufficiently teach or help with leading. In that case, maybe they can delegate one person to get the education and commit the time while everyone else pays to put food on their table. The early leaders of certain organizations would be an example of that extreme situation.

However, as you mentioned, that's not ideal. And if it's not ideal, then we should avoid it if possible, right? In most of the developed world today, it seems perfectly possible. In a certain country, for instance, most people are educated and have some amount of free time. So why not have everyone pitch in to do the work instead of paying one person to do it?

I provided two possible approaches in the original post:

1. Distribute the workload so that no one has to serve full time. This would give everyone an opportunity to earn their own income.

2. Individuals could work diligently and manage their finances wisely to accumulate savings before entering ministry, enabling them to afford to work without compensation.

Additionally, attending a theological school is not the only method to gain education or to effectively lead a congregation. Furthermore, individuals do not need to incur debt to attend a theological school.

If they are doing work then they deserve to be paid.

...unless you're a layperson? As a layperson, I am expected to serve my community while earning my own income, and I am not paid for it. So why pay some people and not others? Is there something fundamentally different between the work that I do and the work that my spiritual leader or music coordinator does?

That's unrealistic

There are a lot of people in various online communities focused on financial independence who would disagree. My partner and I are on schedule to reach financial independence by age 32 on modest salaries. It's really not that hard if you loosen your hold on material pleasure.

How many people do you know

I currently know six individuals who have achieved financial independence before going into ministry so that they could serve without pay.

The things you mentioned seem like reasonable expenses. Of course, every necessary expense for the organization to fulfill its role is justified. By "pocket," I meant the portion that goes directly to an individual for some service that is optional (or could be shared by several people so as not to require compensation).

Because the role of a full-time religious leader is not clearly defined in scripture, the term "full-time pastor" has no concrete meaning to me. As I've seen it practiced, it usually refers to a person who leads the congregation (especially in certain denominations that do not have a system of elders). They prepare at least one sermon per week and possibly a Bible study. They are available day and night to counsel members of the community. They handle many of the administrative tasks of the facility (if the congregation has a building). They serve the local community. They organize meetings outside of the main gathering. They are also typically expected to have a theological education, even though that is not the only way to gain knowledge and is not mandated by scripture.

Meanwhile, many unpaid members of the congregation work full-time jobs in addition to serving the community, leading various aspects of the congregation, and studying scripture/doctrine/theology. At the same time, many other members of the congregation spend their evenings dining out, watching television, and engaging in other unproductive activities.

My point is that many of the laypeople are doing much of the religious leader's work for free, and many more laypeople are available to do the same.

You seemed to imply that more funds lead to a higher salary.

I was not implying that. I was simply stating that the religious leader relies on a constant stream of donations to provide for their basic needs.

No. I just gave that as one example of the potential drawbacks of having paid staff. There are potentially many others, and I'm not sure I could name the primary one.

What prompted this post are a few realizations that I've had over the last couple of years:

1. Reaching financial independence at a young age is quite feasible for anyone in a developed country.

2. The modern proliferation of information means that many more people can gain a religious education by personal study and mentorship outside of formal theological training.

3. Many of the laity do less work for the community because they believe that by funding the organization, they have done their part.

4. Many nonbelievers would love to be part of a loving, serving community but they aren't open to the organization because of financial issues (either rumors or past experiences or suspicion or realistic concerns).

5. I have had the opportunity to participate in a community that has no paid leaders or staff and there has been a long list of tremendous benefits.

6. Some paid leaders live in bigger houses than I can afford.

7. Some paid leaders have really bad personal finance skills.

If your spiritual leader has no training...sounds like a questionable leader.

You seem to be assuming that the only way to be a good counselor or leader or to have sound theological understanding is through formal training. A godly community should naturally produce many good leaders and wise, learned counselors. I think that's the point of, "Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road..."

It's nice that your spiritual guide does all of those things and I'm not saying he shouldn't. My question is, how do you justify compensating him to do those things? Is there no possible alternative? Perhaps:

- eliminating the tasks that are not necessary?
- delegating the tasks to those with free time even if that means training and ordaining more people?
- scheduling a time for questions instead of allowing for the luxury of spontaneity?
- having the community members spend less time studying and more time serving, thus requiring less preparation time?

These are just some ideas. They are not exhaustive and they may not be feasible right now. I'm just trying to propose another (possibly better) way for the future.

You do not appreciate the time it takes to be a proper community leader.

I am a proper community leader, and I am not compensated for it. I also work a full-time secular job. I hear the excuse that it takes too much time, and would like to know what exactly requires a single person to commit so much time and energy that he/she cannot possibly work for money like everyone else.

My partner and I joined last year, but I believe the community has been operating for about eight years. We meet in a very small venue, so when the group grows larger than about 40 people, we have to split into separate meetings, so I'm not sure how many people there are total, but I know they have had to split several times. The group I meet with currently has about 16 people. Being so small, it's a very familial community.

> If you don't have someone calling the shots

What shots? It's organized so that there is never an opportunity for someone to make a unilateral decision. We pray and study together to collectively decide what actions we should take as a community and we take turns volunteering to organize activities as we are available.

> you will soon

What makes you so sure? Is it really that hard to believe that a group of mature, faithful individuals is not dependent on a single paid leader in order to follow a higher purpose?

When your goals are clearly defined, it's usually pretty easy to determine what expenses are necessary to fulfill them. I agree that that will vary as the needs of each community are different.

I also agree that it is not bad (it's great) if someone is able to commit all of their time to serving. In fact, that's my goal when I retire in a few years. The question here is how you justify paying a person who **chose** not to earn money in the usual way when that money could be used to help those in need instead.

It's not impossible

That's the theme that I'm seeing throughout this discussion. It's not impossible to have unpaid staff - it's just harder.

I agree that the usual responsibilities of a spiritual leader are things that must be done. But scripture does not require or even recommend that those jobs be done by just one person or a small group of people. In the early community, very few individuals had the information they needed to fill those roles, so yeah their burden was heavier than that of their followers.

If people are getting lost in the community, there must be a better solution than taking funds that could be used to support the needy to hire a "shepherd." Perhaps splitting into smaller groups?

one of them is to support those teaching the word

Again, it was a practical necessity for the early community. That's simply not the case now. Now it's optional.

I don't see how those other topics relate to this one.

As for asking my spiritual leader, I currently attend a community with no paid staff, so the answer from there is, "It's unnecessary and an unwise use of resources."
Save your money before spending it. That's the secret formula for avoiding all debt.

The difference between this situation and that one is spending one's own money versus spending someone else's donated money.

I don't treat all money with that same high regard - just donated money. People give their money to a religious organization expecting it to be spent responsibly. The organization therefore has an obligation to not only spend it responsibly, but to spend it as responsibly as they possibly can.

I guess I do have a fairly low regard for the expectation to be paid for something that almost everyone else does for free. I understand that it would be an added challenge for leaders to earn their money outside the organization, but perhaps leading is supposed to be more difficult than following. Or perhaps the leaders should be able to rely on help from their supporters.

I have already made the case that it's different today than it was then. It comes down to the economy, and the economies in developed countries today are extremely different from the economy of ancient regions in the first century.

> why not a more democratic structure

That is one solution that I proposed - if we pay one person because he/she is loaded with responsibilities, then couldn't we distribute those responsibilities and eliminate his/her need for compensation? The other solution I proposed would be to keep the same structure and simply not pay the staff. This would cause a subsequent shift where only those who work hardest, spend their money most wisely, save most responsibly, and want to lead for leadership's sake alone (rather than income) would be put in a position of leadership.

I would say that the first solution lowers the bar for leadership, while the second solution raises it.

A third solution might be a combination of the second solution with a slight alteration of the structure so that staff serve only temporarily so that they don't have to achieve full financial independence. They could go back to work after serving full time.

And these are just my ideas; I'm sure that as situations vary, people could be more creative than me in coming up with alternatives to paying leaders.

> would be difficult to replicate without dedicated people

I understand that it is always difficult to transition to a new way of doing things, but it's not impossible. And the fact that something is difficult shouldn't even make us hesitate.

> that's where the elder role is important

Perhaps, but some might say that's where the diversity of the community is important. I've been counseled by leaders, and that's good, but I've also been counseled by community members who have been through similar trials, and that is just as good if not better.

The poor stewardship of money is, again, just one example that I gave of the potential drawbacks of paying leaders. Another potential drawback is highlighted in your example. If I pay someone to fix my plumbing, the assumption is that they do it so that I don't have to. But paying a leader is not the same because, even though I contribute to support them, I am still obligated to serve. Many community members believe that by giving donations their job is done. The teachings of many spiritual leaders did not allow for anyone to hire out the work of the community. The obligation rests on each member.

I meant that (except in special circumstances such as disability) one could work to earn money until one has saved up enough to go to an educational institution without taking on debt. The same applies to paying for vehicles or anything else.
Which principles? That religious leadership should receive compensation? Or that making a living through non-religious work is the more honorable path?

The role of a leader within a religious community is not explicitly defined in sacred texts, though it is suggested that leaders should be righteous. The term for spiritual guides isn't mentioned at all.

Therefore, I don't believe that spiritual leaders or community leaders have fixed roles. I could share examples of how I've seen those roles enacted, but I don't think that's what you're looking for.

I believe a religious community should be structured like a mustard plant. Each part has its own function. While some roles may be more central (you might refer to them as leaders) and others are more outreach-focused, they are all essential to the overall purpose of the plant, which is to produce more plants before its season ends. The parts are not supported by or organized around a solid central structure, nor do they support a central structure. Instead, all parts are closely interwoven, supporting one another. It should not be monolithic and powerful to avoid fostering corruption, as there would be nothing to gain. Additionally, it should not outlive its purpose. Mustard plants are annuals, meaning that once they have fulfilled their purpose, they die. Religious communities should be designed to establish and nurture the next generation of followers, and when they have accomplished their mission, they should be allowed to dissolve or at least transform into something new. When there are full-time leaders who rely on a constant influx of donations to sustain their livelihoods, they can easily become distracted from the community's mission, causing it to overstay its usefulness.

I have to say I definitely did not expect someone to say that here. I'm impressed that you not only believe that, but that you are acting on it. I too hope to plant a community in the next 5-10 years with the same principles. I believe that a lot of disaffected individuals and nonbelievers will find the structure you described refreshing and welcome.

Yes, that is a valid alternative. But you asked me how to avoid debt so I told you. Also, by taking on debt, you have some major disadvantages:

- It costs you a lot more money in the long run because of interest and fees.

- Your debt/income ratio is higher, which means any other loans will require a higher down payment or higher interest rate, again costing you more money in the long run. Or you might not even qualify.

- You risk not getting a job after graduation in which case you can't pay off the loan, so you hurt your credit and the interest grows. Again, costing you more money in the long run. Or you have to get a regular job, just like I suggested except this way you accumulate interest.

- You are dependent on a constant stream of income which could put you in a tight spot if your calling turns out not to be very profitable (e.g. community service).

- You will require a higher salary from your employer than you would otherwise. That is, you will be a greater burden on the organization than you would be if you had just saved up your money.

- Because your income will be provided by the organization, all of these added costs will ultimately be paid by whatever entity you end up serving. Though at that point, it seems like they're serving you.

All of this perpetuates the need to pay the staff, a problem that I pointed out in the original post.

Yes, many people do this with education, vehicles, homes, recreational vehicles, etc. It's popular, but it's not smart. And it's not right to pass on the added costs to faithful supporters.
I think this is pretty well demonstrated by people calling their dogs their children, as if the only difference is the fur. Your human child is not just a pet for your pleasure. He/she is a person.
I would love to meet my great-great-great-grandchild. I love learning about my family history, but it would be so much cooler to know my family's future.

No, a hypocrite is someone who conceals their wrongdoing - a subtle but important distinction for this discussion. Nonetheless, I agree that followers of this faith should not be hypocritical.

The sacred text teaches that believers are called to repent from sin and become a holy (set apart in purity) and perfect (meaning fully grown, not flawless) people. For followers to tell the world that we are no different from society would be contrary to the community's purpose. If we cannot offer a community that is free from hatred, greed, and all the other worldly things, then what are we inviting people into?
I came here to say exactly this. Life after death is uncompelling and largely speculative. Generally, a witness' job is not to speculate, but to speak to what they know of the past and the present.

You're exactly right. A significant religious figure taught a lot of very valuable lessons, but "don't go to hell" was neither the moral of any of the lessons nor the theme of his ministry. If we're to follow this figure's example, hell (whatever it may be) is not for us to worry about.

This is the only comment here that's actually based on scripture. In the religious text, Heaven is the dwelling place of the divine and celestial beings, and certain very special individuals are said to have gone there. The belief that a significant figure allows us to go there is a later formulation. It's not clear which (if any) references to a place of punishment are meant to be taken literally.

There does seem to be some indication of later judgment based on each person's actions, but it's not clear what the outcome will be.
